title: Stereochemistry

read.title: Left hands and right hands
text: A molecule is chiral when it cannot be superimposed on its mirror image, the way a left hand cannot fit a right glove. The usual cause is a carbon with four different groups. 2-Butanol has such a carbon; 2-propanol does not, because its central carbon carries two identical methyl groups.

To label a stereocenter, rank its groups by the atomic number of the atom directly attached. If two atoms tie, move outward until a difference appears, and count each double bond as two single bonds to that atom. Point the lowest-priority group away from you and trace 1 to 2 to 3. Clockwise is R, counterclockwise is S. These labels describe geometry only; they do not predict whether a sample rotates light clockwise (+) or counterclockwise (−).

Mirror-image stereoisomers are enantiomers. They have identical melting points and solubilities, and they differ only in how they interact with polarized light and other chiral things, such as enzymes. Stereoisomers that are not mirror images are diastereomers, and they have different physical properties. A molecule with two stereocenters can have up to four stereoisomers, but tartaric acid has only three: its R,S form contains a mirror plane and is an achiral meso compound.
